chapters.title: Snapshot
chapters.body:
The power-delivery chain feeding the modern AI data centre has become the defining engineering constraint of the computing industry's most consequential infrastructure cycle. As Nvidia's Blackwell GPU racks drew approximately 120 kilowatts each and successor Rubin and Vera-Rubin platforms tracked toward 400–600 kilowatts per rack, the industry's migration from 12-volt to 48-volt intermediate-bus distribution—and the emerging shift toward 800-volt high-voltage direct-current bus architectures—created a structural inflection for the specialty power-conversion sector. No listed pure-play company sits closer to that transition than Vicor Corporation ([NASDAQ: VICR](https://www.vicorpower.com/investors)), the Andover, Massachusetts semiconductor and module company whose Factorized Power Architecture and proprietary ChiP packaging technology were developed, across four decades of founder-directed R&D, precisely for this operating environment.

## Forty-Four Years, One Founder

Dr. Patrizio Vinciarelli founded Vicor in 1981, took it public on NASDAQ in 1990, and has served as Chairman, President, and Chief Executive Officer continuously since—44-plus years, among the longest founder-CEO tenures in the US-listed electronics universe. He controls a reported 20%-plus equity stake, reinforcing the alignment between his convictions about power-conversion architecture and the company's long-term capital allocation. Vicor operates as a vertically integrated specialty power-module IDM: its Andover campus houses its own ChiP (Converter housed in Package) fabrication facility, co-packaging power-management ICs and discrete components at densities that standard foundry-based competitors have not replicated.

The commercial portfolio rests on three platforms: the Factorized Power Architecture—comprising Pre-Regulator Modules (PRMs), Voltage Transformation Modules (VTMs), Multi-phase Current Multipliers (MCMs), and Factorized Bus Converters (FBCs)—targeting 48-volt intermediate-bus and emerging HVDC AI server markets; brick-format DC-DC converters (Maxi, Mini, Micro) serving the industrial, defence, aerospace, and communications installed base that has underwritten profitability through multiple cycles; and the ChiP packaging IP that underlies both.

## An Accelerating Revenue Curve

Fiscal year 2025 marked a meaningful inflection. [Total revenues, including a $45 million patent litigation settlement, reached $452.7 million](https://www.stocktitan.net/news/VICR/vicor-corporation-reports-results-for-the-fourth-quarter-and-year-rl9lbnjhba32.html); product revenues of $350.3 million grew 12.1% year-on-year while royalty revenues of $57.4 million advanced 23.2%. Net income reached $118.6 million ($2.61 diluted EPS) and gross margin expanded to 57.3% from 51.2%, as high-density FPA module shipments scaled alongside near-100%-margin licensing receipts. A fourth-quarter backlog of $176.9 million, up 13.8% year-on-year, indicated demand had not yet cleared.

| Period | Revenue (USD M) | Gross Margin | Backlog (USD M) |
|---|---|---|---|
| FY2024 (implied) | ~$359 | ~51% | — |
| FY2025 | $452.7 | 57.3% | $176.9 |
| Q1 2026 | $113.0 | 55.2% | $300.6 |
| FY2026 (mgmt. guide) | ~$570 | — | — |

The first quarter of 2026 sharpened that picture considerably. [Revenue of $113 million rose 20.2% year-on-year, while the one-year backlog surged 70% sequentially to $300.6 million—a book-to-bill ratio above 2.0x](https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/articles/vicor-corp-vicr-q1-2026-070126700.html). CFO James F. Schmidt guided second-quarter 2026 revenues of "nearly $126 million" and full-year 2026 revenues of "nearly $570 million"—implying roughly 40% growth on the comparable product-plus-royalty revenue base.

## Vertical Power Delivery and the Lead Customer

The commercial catalyst is Vicor's Vertical Power Delivery (VPD) architecture, which places current-multiplier modules within millimetres of the processor die. The [second-generation VPD solution delivers 3 amperes per square millimetre of current density and 40x current multiplication in a 1.5-millimetre package profile](https://www.eenewseurope.com/en/48v-power-for-higher-performance-ai-accelerator-cards/). On the first-quarter 2026 earnings call, Vinciarelli signalled further miniaturisation: "We are not stopping at 1.5 millimeters; we are going thinner, because as we get to power-in-package, it will need to be thinner." A fifth-generation VPD transition for the unnamed lead computing customer—described by President Philip D. Davies as "continuing a steep production ramp of its wafer-scale engine with best-in-class AI inference performance," language analysts have associated with Cerebras Systems though Vicor did not confirm—was expected in the second half of 2026.

Andover's capacity is the binding constraint. Management indicated Vicor expected "to remain capacity constrained for a substantial timeframe," and raised Fab 1's annualised revenue throughput target to at least $1.5 billion while planning a second facility in an existing building for faster deployment, with a secondary 3Di production line scheduled for the third or fourth quarter of 2026.

## Patent Fortress

Vicor's IP position is defended aggressively. In [February 2025, the International Trade Commission issued a Final Determination in Investigation No. 337-TA-1370](https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2025/02/14/3026816/0/en/ITC-bars-importation-of-power-modules-and-unlicensed-computing-systems-that-infringe-Vicor-patents.html), upholding U.S. Patent Nos. 9,516,761 and 9,166,481 as valid and infringed, and issuing Limited Exclusion Orders against Delta Electronics (Americas), Quanta Computer USA, FII USA, and Ingrasys Technology USA—barring importation of unlicensed power modules and computing systems into the United States. The [Patent Trial and Appeal Board had denied all three Delta-filed Inter Partes Review petitions in May 2024](https://www.vicorpower.com/press-room/2024/vicor-patents-asserted-against-infringing-nbms-withstand-validity-challenges), ruling that Delta had not established a reasonable likelihood of prevailing on validity grounds. Vicor booked a $45 million settlement in 2025; management projected the broader enforcement framework would contribute nearly $300 million in cumulative licensing revenues through 2026. Vinciarelli has characterised licensing as "nearly 100% margin in terms of profitability."

This dossier examines whether that structural positioning translates into a durable franchise: the AI data centre revenue conversion trajectory from a $300 million backlog; 48-volt VRM and 800-volt HVDC product roadmap execution as rack power densities escalate; the durability of the ITC exclusion-order framework against appeals and potential design-arounds; competitive positioning against Monolithic Power Systems, Infineon, Power Integrations, and Navitas; and whether 44 years of founder-controlled governance serves shareholders through the steepest demand cycle the company has yet encountered.

chapters.title: From 1981 founding through 1990 IPO to the AI 48V/HVDC inflection
chapters.body:
## The Physicist at the Bench

The route from particle physics to power conversion is not an obvious one, but for Dr. Patrizio Vinciarelli it traced a clean arc. Born in Rome and educated at Sapienza University, Vinciarelli spent the first decade of his professional life working at the frontier of fundamental physics — first as a fellow at CERN in Geneva from 1973 to 1976, where he published on soliton models of hadrons, then at Stanford, and finally at Princeton's Institute for Advanced Study from 1977 to 1980, where he also served as a university instructor. It was there, at the edge of theoretical physics, that he encountered the boundary he would spend the rest of his career dismantling.

By his own account, Vinciarelli grew frustrated with the pace of progress in his particular academic field. The pivot he chose was characterised less by abandonment than by redirection: he applied the same rigour that had served him in high-energy physics to the decidedly applied problem of moving electrical energy from one voltage to another as efficiently, densely, and reliably as possible. Existing power-conversion solutions, he concluded, "were primitive and lacked scalability." On April 2, 1981, he incorporated Vicor Corporation in Andover, Massachusetts, to prove otherwise. Seed capital arrived, notably, from Nobel Prize-winning physicists — an origin story that set the intellectual tone of the company Vinciarelli would lead, without interruption, for the next four and a half decades.

The company's first three years were spent entirely in development. The flagship insight was zero-current switching (ZCS) — a topology that allowed power transistors to switch at megahertz-range frequencies with dramatically lower losses than conventional designs, because the switching events occurred when the current through the device was at or near zero. It was a fundamentally new approach to the electromagnetic trade-offs that govern converter size, weight, and efficiency. The engineering translation from theoretical topology to manufacturable product took until 1984, when Vicor shipped its first commercial converter: a device delivering 25 watts per cubic inch, roughly twenty times denser than anything then commercially available. [Vicor IR](https://www.vicorpower.com/resource-library/articles/patrizio-vinciarelli-creates-vicor) The first product planted a flag on a density frontier that Vinciarelli would spend the ensuing decades continuously advancing — modern Vicor products now achieve approximately 10,000 watts per cubic inch, representing, in his words, "a three orders of magnitude increase from 1980 levels."

## The Brick-Converter Franchise and the 1990 IPO

The first generation of Vicor products formalised into what became the Maxi, Mini, and Micro brick families — a standardised form-factor framework for DC-DC power modules that gave customers a drop-in solution across a wide range of input and output voltage combinations. The brick concept was not merely an engineering convenience; it was a market architecture, one that allowed Vicor to build a repeatable franchise across industrial, defence, communications, and data-processing end markets. The brick families established what became the company's core commercial identity through the late 1980s and 1990s.

In 1990, Vicor listed on the NASDAQ National Market System under the ticker VICR, raising the capital that funded a significant expansion in manufacturing capacity at the Andover campus and the opening of sales offices in Europe and Asia. By the early 1990s, the company had established technical support centres in Germany (1990) and Taiwan (1994), with France, Italy, Hong Kong, and England following by 1995. The global footprint was built to serve a customer base that was itself globalising — telecommunications infrastructure buildouts, defence electronics programmes, and the accelerating proliferation of microprocessor-based industrial systems all created sustained demand for the Maxi/Mini/Micro franchise. Revenues surpassed $100 million during this period as international sales grew into a meaningful proportion of the total.

The commercial durability of the brick franchise was underwritten by an aggressive patent posture. Vinciarelli, who would ultimately hold more than 150 US patents in power electronics, was the named inventor on the foundational ZCS patents that defined the product line. That IP position drew its first serious legal test at the end of the decade, as the brick-converter market matured and competitors sought to challenge the underlying claims.

## The Patent Litigation Decade

Beginning in 2000, Vicor and its subsidiary VLT, Inc. filed a series of patent-infringement actions in the US District Court for the District of Massachusetts against a cohort of power-supply rivals — Lucent Technologies, Artesyn Technologies, Lambda Electronics, Tyco Electronics, and Power-One. The central patent at issue, Vicor's Reissue Patent No. 36,098, covered reset circuitry fundamental to high-frequency power conversion. In January 2002, the district court granted Vicor a $20 million attachment of Lucent's assets as a preliminary measure, finding that Vicor had "a reasonable likelihood of succeeding in its claim of patent infringement" and that $20 million represented "a conservative estimate of actual damages." In 2004, the US Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit affirmed the lower court's rulings in Vicor's favour across the five cases — validating the patent claims, rejecting indefiniteness challenges, and sustaining Vicor's claim construction. [Law360](https://www.law360.com/articles/1510/appeals-court-rules-for-vicor-in-power-patent-suits)

The Federal Circuit victory did not end Vicor's litigation posture — it established it as a permanent feature of the company's competitive strategy. As successive generations of packaging and architecture IP displaced the original brick portfolio, the company maintained a consistent willingness to defend new patents through the courts.

## Factorized Power and the ChiP Era

By the early 2000s, the brick-converter market faced a structural headwind: as microprocessor voltages fell below 1.5 V and load currents climbed toward hundreds of amperes, a monolithic converter topology could not efficiently bridge the gap from a 48-volt bus to a sub-volt, high-current processor rail. Vicor's answer was the Factorized Power Architecture (FPA), introduced in 2003 — a design philosophy that separated the regulation function from the transformation function, assigning each to a dedicated module optimised for its specific role. [Vicor whitepaper](https://www.vicorpower.com/documents/whitepapers/wp-FPA-Achieving-high-density-efficiency-VICOR.pdf)

Under FPA, a Pre-Regulator Module (PRM) handles voltage regulation from the bus, while a Voltage Transformation Module (VTM) — initially built around a Sine Amplitude Converter (SAC) topology introduced in 2008 — performs the step-down transformation at very high frequency and very high efficiency. The VTM acts as a current multiplier: a modest-current regulated bus voltage enters one end, and a high-current processor voltage exits the other. Multi-phase Current Multipliers (MCMs) followed, enabling parallel current delivery at scales approaching 1,000 amperes per module. The modular separation of regulation and transformation was architecturally radical — it allowed each function to be optimised independently and placed closer to the load.

The packaging technology that embodied FPA went through two generational transitions. The VI Chip, launched in 2008 as a one-inch-square overmoulded PCB module with J-lead pins, was the first vehicle for the new architecture and quickly found application in IBM supercomputer programmes requiring sub-1 V, high-current power. In 2015, Vicor rebuilt the package from first principles, producing the Converter housed in Package (ChiP) — modules cut from fixed-size panels in a process explicitly analogous to how silicon chips are diced from wafers. The two-sided assembly method, combined with advances in control systems and materials, compressed the power density to 10,000 W/in³ in the most recent generations and enabled current-delivery specifications approaching 1,000 amperes per module. By 2025, the company was pursuing Vertical Power Delivery (VPD) — three-dimensionally stacked ChiP assemblies that position the power converter directly against the processor package, reducing resistance in the last 1.5 millimetres of the power-delivery path. At the Q1 2026 earnings call, Vinciarelli described second-generation VPD specifications of 3 A/mm² current density, up to 40× current multiplication, and a 1.5-millimetre package thickness, adding: "we're not stopping at 1.5 millimeter, we're going thinner."

## The 48V/HVDC Inflection

The arrival of GPU-accelerated AI workloads at hyperscale data centres restructured the power-delivery calculus in ways that converged on the architectural choices Vicor had been making for two decades. Nvidia Blackwell racks at approximately 120 kW per rack rendered conventional 12V distribution architecturally untenable — distribution losses at 12V scale as the square of the current, and the currents required to feed a 120 kW rack at 12V are physically impractical in a rack cable harness. The transition to 48V intermediate-bus distribution, which Vicor had championed since the mid-2000s, reduced distribution losses by a factor of sixteen relative to 12V. Google and Nvidia adopted the 48V standard; the installed base of FPA-compatible hardware began converting from a niche high-performance computing franchise into a mainstream data-centre infrastructure position.

The financial consequences became visible in the fiscal-year comparisons. Product revenues in FY2024 reached $359.1 million. [SEC EDGAR 10-K FY2024](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0000751978/000095017025030619/vicr-20241231.htm) In FY2025, total net revenues reached $452.7 million — including $57.4 million in royalties, of which $45 million reflected a patent-litigation settlement — as Advanced Products climbed to 61% of product revenue. By Q1 2026, the company's backlog stood at $301 million, up 70% sequentially, a 2.7× backlog-to-revenue ratio that Vinciarelli described by stating that Vicor saw itself "being essentially sold out in terms of capacity for the foreseeable future." Fab 1 in Andover was on a path from $1 billion to $1.5 billion per year in capacity, and the company had accelerated plans for a second fab in an existing building to avoid the timeline of ground-up construction.

The IP enforcement machinery ran in parallel. In July 2023, Vicor filed a Section 337 complaint at the US International Trade Commission (Investigation No. 337-TA-1370), targeting power converter modules and the computing systems containing them. In September 2024, Administrative Law Judge Cameron Elliot issued an Initial Determination finding violations of US Patent Nos. 9,516,761 and 9,166,481. On February 13, 2025, the ITC issued its Final Determination: a Limited Exclusion Order barring all named respondents from importing infringing modules, and Cease and Desist Orders against Delta Electronics (Americas), Quanta Computer, FII USA, and Ingrasys Technology. [ITC press release via Vicor IR](https://vicorcorporation.gcs-web.com/news-releases/news-release-details/itc-bars-importation-power-modules-and-unlicensed-computing) The pattern — foundational innovation, proprietary packaging, sustained litigation defence, eventual enforcement — had completed another cycle, forty-four years after Vinciarelli first brought his physicist's methodology to bear on the problem of moving electrons efficiently from one voltage to another.

---

chapters.title: Factorized Power Architecture, ChiP packaging, brick converters, and the 48V → 800V HVDC roadmap
chapters.body:
## The Factorization Principle

When Patrizio Vinciarelli filed the foundational patents underpinning what Vicor would eventually market as the Factorized Power Architecture, the central insight was deceptively simple: voltage regulation and voltage transformation are separate physical problems, and conflating them in a single converter imposes penalties that compound as power density rises. Conventional switching power supplies performed both functions simultaneously — they regulated the output voltage while also stepping it down from the input rail. Vinciarelli's approach disaggregated the two. A Pre-Regulator Module handles tight voltage regulation on the intermediate bus; a Voltage Transformation Module performs high-ratio step-down conversion at near-ideal efficiency with no feedback loop of its own. The result is a power architecture where each stage does one thing exceptionally well, and the system-level product — efficiency, power density, thermal footprint — exceeds what a monolithic converter can achieve.

The FPA product taxonomy that Vicor developed across decades of iteration reflects this two-stage logic. PRMs regulate the intermediate bus — typically 48V — from a wide-range input, absorbing line and load transients through a control loop that the downstream VTM never needs to see. VTMs then perform fixed-ratio transformation from the regulated intermediate bus to point-of-load voltages, operating as sine-amplitude converters that recirculate reactive energy rather than dissipating it, yielding efficiencies that can approach 97 percent in production silicon. Multi-phase Current Multipliers extend this architecture to sub-volt, multi-hundred-ampere point-of-load conversion required by modern AI accelerators, while Factorized Bus Converters provide the 48V bus conversion stage for rack-level distribution. The taxonomy is not marketing taxonomy; each module occupies a distinct place in the conversion chain with its own optimization target.

## ChiP Packaging: The Manufacturing Substrate

The physical realization of this architecture depends on packaging technology that Vicor spent decades developing and protecting. The ChiP — Converter housed in Package — format is a proprietary multi-chip module structure that integrates power semiconductors, passive components, magnetic elements, and control ICs into a flat, surface-mountable package. Where most power modules are assembled from discrete components on a substrate, ChiP packaging co-fabricates the magnetics and semiconductor die within a single laminated structure, enabling power densities that surface-mount discrete assembly cannot match.

The engineering consequence is visible in the product lineup. A ChiP-packaged VTM occupying a footprint comparable to a large surface-mount integrated circuit can deliver tens of amperes at multi-megahertz switching frequencies, with thermal paths engineered directly into the package lid. The high switching frequencies enabled by the integrated magnetics reduce the size of energy-storage elements, which in turn allow the flat package geometry. It is a self-reinforcing design loop: planar magnetics allow high frequency, high frequency allows small passives, small passives allow flat packaging, flat packaging enables system-level board density.

Vicor has defended this technology through repeated patent litigation, regarding ChiP as the manufacturing moat that makes the FPA product line difficult to replicate without infringing its IP estate. The company has pursued enforcement actions against competitors over multiple cycles, accepting litigation expense as the price of maintaining a protected position in high-density converter packaging. Settlement proceeds from concluded litigation have appeared periodically in Vicor's financial statements as episodic income items, partially offsetting the legal costs of enforcement.

## Brick Converters: The Installed Base

Long before the FPA family reached volume production, Vicor's revenue base rested on the brick DC-DC converter families that the company pioneered in the 1980s and 1990s. The Maxi, Mini, and Micro brick form factors established an industry-standard mechanical footprint that competitors eventually adopted, creating an installed base spanning industrial automation, defense electronics, telecommunications infrastructure, and medical equipment. Brick converters accept a wide-range DC input — typically 28V or 48V on the bus, in some cases military 270V — and deliver regulated, isolated DC output to the load.

The defense segment has been a consistent buyer. Platforms from Lockheed Martin, RTX, and Northrop Grumman integrate Vicor bricks in avionic and ground-vehicle power systems where the combination of isolation, wide input range, and reliability across temperature extremes is specified. The industrial and communications segments provide additional baseline demand that insulates Vicor's revenue from the volatility of any single end market. This installed base matters in a product architecture sense as well: the manufacturing processes and quality systems developed to meet military and industrial reliability specifications transferred directly to the ChiP packaging line, where the thermal-cycling and mechanical-stress requirements are equally demanding.

The brick families are mature product lines, and Vicor does not expect them to drive growth at the rate of the FPA and AI-oriented products. But they generate recurring revenue, carry relatively predictable margins once tooled, and support the operating cost base of the Andover manufacturing campus through cycles when data center demand is lumpy.

## 48V: The Architecture Transition

The shift from 12V to 48V intermediate-bus architecture in AI server platforms has been the most consequential market transition in Vicor's history, and it is still in progress. The physics are straightforward: at a given power level, doubling the bus voltage halves the current, reducing resistive I²R losses in bus bars, PCB copper, and connectors by a factor of four. As GPU rack power climbed from the roughly 10–20 kW of mid-tier deep-learning inference servers toward the 120 kW-class racks enabled by Nvidia's Blackwell GB200 NVL72 architecture, the losses on a 12V distribution bus became structurally untenable. A 120 kW rack operating at 12V would require approximately 10,000 amperes of bus current — mechanically and thermally impractical at production rack form factors.

The 48V intermediate bus eliminates this constraint. At 48V, the same 120 kW rack requires approximately 2,500 amperes, a figure that commodity copper distribution can handle. Vicor's FPA is architecturally native to this bus voltage in a way that many competitors' product lines are not: the VTM family was designed from the outset to operate from a 48V intermediate bus, stepping down to the sub-volt GPU core voltages in a single high-ratio conversion stage without the intermediate 12V conversion step that legacy two-stage architectures require.

The 48V VRM opportunity at GPU rack level is the principal commercial prize Vicor has pursued since approximately 2020. Server OEMs integrating Nvidia and AMD accelerator platforms must source power modules capable of delivering current at GPU core voltages — often below one volt, with transient demands in the hundreds of amperes — directly from the 48V bus. Vicor's MCM and VTM products target this conversion stage. The design-in cycle for server platforms runs eighteen to thirty-six months from initial engagement to volume production, which is why Vicor's management has discussed AI data center engagement for several years ahead of the volume revenue recognition that the forward analyst consensus anticipates.

## 800V HVDC: The Next Inflection

The 48V transition is being followed by a second, more radical architectural shift that Vicor has positioned itself to address: the move to 800V high-voltage DC distribution within the data center facility itself. The conventional data center power chain runs from the utility AC feed through a transformer and UPS, down to a 480V AC distribution bus, into rack-level power distribution units that perform AC-to-DC conversion and supply 48V to the server platforms. Each conversion stage carries losses. Eliminating the final AC-to-DC stage by distributing 800V DC directly to the rack reduces conversion losses and simplifies the power chain.

Nvidia's infrastructure teams have disclosed plans for 800V HVDC distribution in next-generation hyperscale data center designs, with timelines that put initial deployments in the 2025–2027 window. For Vicor, this creates an opportunity at the rack entry point: a PRM capable of accepting 800V DC input and regulating it to the 48V intermediate bus would sit at the top of the conversion chain, immediately downstream of the facility's HVDC bus. The FPA's PRM stage is designed for this role — it is a high-ratio step-down regulator that can be configured for wide input-range operation, and the separation of regulation from transformation means the downstream VTM and MCM stages are indifferent to whether the upstream bus comes from a 48V charger or a PRM fed from 800V HVDC.

Vicor's management has been explicit about this positioning in investor communications. The company views the 48V-to-800V HVDC progression as a multi-year runway rather than a single product cycle, because each architectural transition requires new design-ins at the server, rack, and facility level — all of which run on long qualification timescales that protect incumbents who achieve early design wins.

## Andover: The Vertical Fab as Competitive Moat

The products and architectures described above are manufactured at a single campus in Andover, Massachusetts, where Vicor operates as a vertically integrated specialty power-module IDM. The Andover facility houses semiconductor fabrication, ChiP packaging and assembly, and final test under one roof — an unusual configuration for a company of Vicor's scale, which typically characterizes fabless or fab-lite models in the analog and power semiconductor universe.

The vertical integration reflects Vinciarelli's conviction that proprietary process technology is inseparable from product differentiation. The ChiP packaging process, with its integrated planar magnetics and co-packaged die structures, cannot be transferred to a contract manufacturer without exposing the process know-how that underlies Vicor's density and efficiency claims. The Andover fab gives Vicor direct control over process yields, packaging quality, and capacity allocation — critical variables when a large customer's server program depends on Vicor meeting a qualification deadline.

Capacity expansion at Andover through 2024 and 2025, disclosed in Vicor's capital expenditure guidance across its 10-K and quarterly filings, represents the company's bet on AI data center demand conversion. The fixed cost base of a vertical fab creates significant operating leverage: incremental revenue at high utilization flows to operating income at margins that are not available at lower utilization rates. This leverage is the mechanism by which the AI data center design-in cycle, once converted to volume production, would produce a financial profile materially different from Vicor's historical $300–400 million revenue band — and it is the reason investors have assigned a premium multiple to the stock relative to the company's current earnings run rate.

chapters.title: Revenue trajectory, AI mix shift, operating leverage, capital structure
chapters.body:
Four years ago, Vicor's annual revenue stood at $399 million—profitable, but trapped in the cyclical rhythms of industrial and defense electronics. By the close of FY2025, that figure had risen to $452.7 million, and the composition of the business had shifted in ways that made the headline number almost secondary. A 48V/HVDC power-architecture transition driven by AI data center buildout, the maturation of a decades-long patent portfolio into a freestanding royalty income stream, and the operating leverage latent in Vicor's vertically integrated Andover campus had begun to assert themselves simultaneously. The financial story of 2022 through early 2026 is not a smooth acceleration; it is a trough-and-inflection narrative, and the inflection is still unfolding.

## Revenue Trajectory, FY2022–FY2025

The four-year revenue arc obscures more than it reveals at first glance.

| Fiscal Year | Net Revenue | YoY Change | Gross Margin | Operating Income/(Loss) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| FY2022 | $399.1M | — | 45.2% | $27.2M (6.8%) |
| FY2023 | $405.1M | +1.5% | 50.6% | $51.4M (12.7%) |
| FY2024 | $359.1M | −11.4% | 51.2% | ($1.3M) |
| FY2025 | $452.7M | +26.1% | 57.3% | $81.8M (18.1%) |

*Sources: [VICR 10-K FY2022](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0000751978/000119312523053976/d425264d10k.htm), [FY2023](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0000751978/000095017024022018/vicr-20231231.htm), [FY2024](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0000751978/000095017025030619/vicr-20241231.htm), [FY2025](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0000751978/000119312526085102/vicr-20251231.htm)*

FY2022 was a record at the time but carried a compressed 45.2% gross margin—the lowest in the period—reflecting elevated capacity spend at Andover ahead of demand absorption and a product mix still weighted toward lower-margin brick converters. Operating income reached only $27.2 million on $399 million of revenue, a 6.8% margin that illustrated just how capital-intensive the IDM model is when utilization lags. FY2023 brought a modest 1.5% revenue gain to $405.1 million, but a more significant story in profitability: gross margin expanded to 50.6% and operating income nearly doubled to $51.4 million as Advanced Products—Vicor's label for FPA-architecture modules and ChiP-packaged VPDs—improved their absorption of the fixed-cost base. Licensing revenue, still nascent, contributed $15.9 million in FY2023 versus only $2.8 million the prior year, an early signal of what was to come.

FY2024 was the trough. Net revenue fell 11.4% to $359.1 million as inventory digestion swept through industrial, communications, and defense channels simultaneously, and as Vicor's second-generation Vertical Power Delivery (VPD) solutions for AI servers encountered ASIC development delays that pushed volume shipments into 2025. Operating expenses as a percentage of revenue swelled to 51.6%—up from 37.9% in FY2023—absorbing almost the entirety of a 51.2% gross margin and producing an operating loss of $1.3 million for the year. Net income survived at $6.1 million only through below-the-line offsets. The quarter-by-quarter cadence within FY2024 told the recovery story, however: Q1 revenue was $83.9 million; by Q4 it had reached $96.2 million (+3.8% year-on-year), the first consecutive sequential improvements since the digestion trough, and gross margin in Q4 2024 came in at 52.4%.

FY2025 delivered the inflection. Full-year revenue of $452.7 million comprised $350.3 million in product revenue (+4.1% year-on-year), $57.4 million in royalty revenue (+23.2%), and a $45 million patent litigation settlement recognized in the second quarter. Excluding the settlement, net product and royalty revenue reached $407.7 million—above FY2023's record and accelerating through the back half of the year.

## The AI Mix Shift and Licensing Inflection

Vicor reports product revenue in two segments: Advanced Products, which encompasses FPA-architecture modules, ChiP-packaged VPDs, and related AI and high-performance computing solutions; and Brick Products, the legacy DC-DC converter families serving industrial, defense, and communications customers.

In FY2022, Advanced Products represented approximately 61% of consolidated product revenue; Brick held the remaining 39%. Through FY2023 and FY2024 that balance compressed as AI design-in cycles lagged and inventory digestion disproportionately hit the computing supply chain. By Q3 FY2025 the mix had reasserted itself: Advanced Products contributed $65.5 million (+32.6% year-on-year) against Brick's $44.9 million (+2.6%), returning Advanced to a 59% revenue share of the product mix. The differential growth rates—32.6% versus 2.6%—capture the structural demand wedge opening between AI server power architecture and traditional electronics markets.

Alongside product mix, the royalty line has emerged as a structurally distinct revenue pillar. Licensing revenue grew from $2.8 million in FY2022 to $15.9 million in FY2023 and reached a run-rate of $57.4 million in FY2025 (exclusive of the $45 million one-time settlement). The catalyst was a multi-front ITC enforcement campaign that culminated in FY2025 with a Limited Exclusion Order banning the importation of infringing bus converters and computing systems into the United States. With two of an eventual six major AI-computing licensees signed as of the Q4 2025 earnings call, Vicor has guided toward nearly $300 million in cumulative licensing revenue through 2026, a figure Vinciarelli placed in context on the [February 2026 Q4 earnings call](https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2026/02/19/vicor-vicr-q4-2025-earnings-call-transcript/):

> "We expect hundreds of millions of dollars of revenues from a lot of things. And the $45,000,000 event last year is, in hindsight, going to be another drop in the bucket."

The $200 to $400 per-XPU content estimate Vicor management cited for its Gen 5 VPD solutions—serving Blackwell-class and emerging Vera-Rubin rack densities—frames a discrete revenue opportunity that royalties and product shipments will together address. In Q3 FY2025, [Vicor announced](https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2025/10/20/3169740/0/en/Vicor-steps-up-its-IP-licensing-practice.html) that quarterly licensing revenues had exceeded its quarterly R&D investment, a milestone underscoring how materially the portfolio has monetized.

## Operating Leverage and Gross Margin Progression

The gross margin trajectory from 45.2% in FY2022 to 57.3% in FY2025 reflects three concurrent forces: product mix enrichment as Advanced Products displace lower-margin Brick in the revenue mix; capacity utilization leverage on the Andover IDM campus; and the high-flow-through royalty and settlement revenues that carry near-100% incremental gross margin.

The IDM model is a double-edged instrument. When revenue scales, the fixed cost base at Andover—internal fab, packaging, and test—delivers operating leverage that fabless competitors cannot match because it is embedded in margin rather than reported separately as capacity fees. When revenue falls, as in FY2024, those same fixed costs compress margins and turn operating income negative with speed. The 51.2% gross margin the company held through FY2024's $359 million trough revenue was respectable precisely because the IDM model keeps pure product margins relatively stable even as volumes decline; the operating-income damage was inflicted primarily through elevated operating-expense ratios rather than gross margin collapse.

By Q4 FY2025, with product revenue running at $92.7 million per quarter and the royalty stream supplementing it, Andover was approaching 80% utilization—a threshold Vinciarelli has characterized as equivalent to an approximately $800 million annualized revenue run-rate capacity at the existing campus. Full buildout capacity of the Andover facility exceeds $1 billion in annual product revenue. To bridge beyond that level, Vicor disclosed at the Q4 2025 call that it had received two site offers for a second manufacturing facility, with management evaluating a new build versus acquisition and estimating a potential 18-month acceleration in timeline relative to a greenfield project. The capital decision remained open as of the May 2026 frozen snapshot.

## Capital Structure: Cash Accumulation and Minimal Debt

Vicor's balance sheet is a study in conservative financial architecture. The company carries minimal long-term debt, a posture that has persisted across multiple capital expenditure cycles and litigation battles. Cash and equivalents have compounded steadily: $190.6 million at end-FY2022, $242.2 million at end-FY2023, approximately $267 million at end of Q3 FY2024, and $402.8 million at end-FY2025—the step-up in the final year reflecting the $45 million settlement receipt, accelerating royalty generation, and improved operating cash flow as product revenue recovered. With diluted shares of approximately 45.5 million, the end-FY2025 cash position of $402.8 million represents roughly $8.85 per share in cash against a stock that has traded well above book value on the expectation of the IP licensing pipeline conversion.

Full-year FY2025 net income reached $118.6 million, or $2.61 per diluted share—versus $6.1 million in FY2024—though the figure reflects both the $45 million patent settlement and a material non-recurring deferred tax benefit recognized in Q4 2025. Operating income of $81.8 million, representing an 18.1% operating margin, is the cleaner measure of underlying business leverage and the highest operating margin in the four-year period.

## The Founder's Lock

Vicor's capital structure carries a dimension that has no analog among power semiconductor peers: Patrizio Vinciarelli's effective control of the enterprise through a dual-class share structure that insulates the company's strategic direction from institutional or activist pressure across any conceivable time horizon.

As of the [2025 DEF 14A proxy statement](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0000751978/000095017025060646/vicr-20250430.htm), Vinciarelli holds 79.6% of total voting power, derived from his ownership of Class B Common Stock—which carries ten votes per share—alongside his Common Stock holdings. As of March 31, 2025, there were 33.5 million shares of Common Stock and 11.7 million shares of Class B Common Stock outstanding. Institutional investors hold approximately 60.8% of the economic interest in Common Stock, with JPMorgan, BlackRock, and Vanguard among the largest common holders, but their aggregate voting power is structurally subordinate. No proxy contest, hostile acquirer, or shareholder resolution can displace Vinciarelli's R&D priorities or IP enforcement strategy without his consent.

## Entering 2026: Backlog, Guidance, and the IP Pipeline

The forward indicators entering the frozen snapshot window were unambiguous in their direction. [Q1 FY2026 results](https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2026/05/03/vicor-vicr-q1-2026-earnings-transcript/), reported on May 3, 2026, showed revenue of $113.0 million—a 20.2% year-on-year increase and a 5.3% sequential advance from Q4 2025. Gross margin was 55.2%, representing 800 basis points of improvement year-on-year even without a settlement benefit. Book-to-bill exceeded 2.0 for the quarter, and the one-year backlog surged 70% sequentially to $300.6 million. Management issued full-year FY2026 revenue guidance of approximately $570 million—a figure that explicitly excluded revenues from any new licensing agreements pending a second ITC case determination expected in 2027, meaning it rests on conservative IP assumptions. Net income for Q1 2026 was $20.7 million, or $0.44 per diluted share.

Vinciarelli's characterization of 2026 at the Q4 2025 earnings call—*"a year of major increase in product revenue…at a level that we have not enjoyed for quite some time"*—proved, within one reporting cycle, to be an understatement.

---

*Primary sources: [VICR 10-K FY2022](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0000751978/000119312523053976/d425264d10k.htm) · [FY2023](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0000751978/000095017024022018/vicr-20231231.htm) · [FY2024](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0000751978/000095017025030619/vicr-20241231.htm) · [FY2025](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0000751978/000119312526085102/vicr-20251231.htm) · [Q4 2025 Earnings Call Transcript](https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2026/02/19/vicor-vicr-q4-2025-earnings-call-transcript/) · [Q1 2026 Earnings Transcript](https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2026/05/03/vicor-vicr-q1-2026-earnings-transcript/) · [DEF 14A 2025](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0000751978/000095017025060646/vicr-20250430.htm) · [Vicor steps up IP licensing practice](https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2025/10/20/3169740/0/en/Vicor-steps-up-its-IP-licensing-practice.html)*

chapters.title: Valuation — multiples, peer comparison, and bull/base/bear scenarios
chapters.body:
## A Valuation Without a Clean Comp

Vicor occupies an uncomfortable position in the portfolio of screening tools that most institutional investors use. It is not a diversified analog semiconductor company in the Texas Instruments mould, nor a high-multiple power-management IC franchise in the Monolithic Power Systems tradition, nor a mature brick-converter incumbent commanding conservative multiples. It is a founder-controlled specialty module company with a forty-year IP franchise, a vertically integrated fab in Andover that creates both operating leverage and fixed-cost exposure, and a revenue trajectory that — after years of frustrating the AI thesis — appears through the frozen-snapshot window of May 2026 to be entering a genuine volume-conversion phase. Pricing that compound of attributes requires judgment, not a screener.

## Current Multiples and Market Capitalization

Vicor carries a share count of approximately 43–44 million diluted shares as of its most recent proxy and quarterly disclosures. Exact market data at the frozen snapshot date of 23 May 2026 requires inference: VICR's trailing twelve-month price range through early 2026 likely spanned a wide band consistent with the company's historical volatility profile, with the stock having traded in the mid-$40s to low-$80s range as AI-design-in conversion moved from disclosure to delivery. Reasoning from a mid-range price of approximately $65–70 per share yields an indicative market capitalisation of roughly $2.8–3.1 billion.

With minimal reported debt and a cash-and-equivalents position estimated in the $200–275 million range — funded by cumulative operating profitability and episodic patent-settlement receipts across prior cycles — the enterprise value sits meaningfully below headline market cap, at roughly $2.5–2.9 billion. On the basis of FY2025 revenue tracking toward the upper end of the $300–400 million range (approximately $380–400 million), that implies a trailing EV/Revenue of roughly 6–7x. For a business with disclosed gross margins in the 40–50% range depending on product mix, and operating margin leverage that is a direct function of Andover fab utilisation, the premium is explicable only if forward revenue acceleration is credited.

Forward multiples depend heavily on the FY2026 revenue assumption. If AI design-ins convert at the pace the company's customer-engagement disclosures suggest — with Nvidia Blackwell-era 48V rack architectures and emerging 800V HVDC programmes driving module attach rates at hyperscaler and server-OEM customers — forward revenue could plausibly reach $460–540 million. On that range, EV/Revenue compresses toward 5–6x, still carrying a specialty-technology premium over commodity power. A forward P/E in the 35–50x range is implied, depending on whether operating leverage materialises or is consumed by continued Andover capacity investment. The PEG ratio, on any credible growth assumption, sits below 2x for the first time in several years.

## Historical Multiple Range: De-Rating and Recovery

VICR's own multiple history provides the most instructive context. At the 2021 cycle peak — when the company's FPA and 48V positioning first entered broad analyst awareness — the stock briefly touched valuations implying 80–100x trailing earnings and EV/Revenue above 10x, reflecting genuine momentum-buyer enthusiasm. The subsequent disappointment through 2022–2023, as enterprise server buildout plateaued and AI inference volumes remained concentrated in a handful of early hyperscaler programs, produced a de-rating that compressed multiples toward 20–30x forward P/E and EV/Revenue below 5x by early 2024.

The recovery through 2024–2025 has been partial and uneven — more consistent with a re-rating on fundamental delivery than a momentum re-run. The stock remained volatile around each earnings release as investors tried to distinguish genuine AI design-in revenue from the structural "design wins but not yet shipping" narrative that defined 2022–2023. By the frozen-snapshot window, the multiple structure appears to reflect a market that has partially — but not fully — credited the forward revenue trajectory.

## Peer-Group Multiple Comparison

The table below positions VICR's estimated multiples against five named peers from the competitive and sector-adjacent set, using approximate figures consistent with the frozen-snapshot period. Estimates for peers carry the same inference caveats noted above.

| Company | Ticker | Forward P/E | EV/EBITDA | EV/Revenue | P/B | Category |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Vicor** | VICR | ~38–48x | ~22–30x | ~5–7x | ~5–8x | AI power modules, FPA / ChiP |
| Monolithic Power Systems | MPWR | ~45–58x | ~30–38x | ~12–16x | ~10–16x | AI power management ICs |
| Power Integrations | POWI | ~20–26x | ~13–18x | ~3–5x | ~3–5x | Specialty AC-DC power |
| Navitas Semiconductor | NVTS | NM | NM | ~3–5x | ~1–2x | GaN, pre-profitability |
| Texas Instruments | TXN | ~22–28x | ~14–20x | ~5–8x | ~8–14x | Diversified analog |
| Analog Devices | ADI | ~26–34x | ~18–25x | ~6–9x | ~3–5x | Diversified analog / signal chain |

Several observations emerge from the comparison. First, VICR's EV/Revenue multiple is notably lower than MPWR's, reflecting both Monolithic Power's superior gross-margin profile — its fabless model avoids the Andover fixed-cost base — and its deeper penetration of high-volume AI server power-management design wins already recognised in revenue. The VICR discount is partly deserved, partly a lag: if Andover throughput scales with AI demand, the operating leverage dynamic could rapidly compress the gap. Second, VICR commands a meaningful premium over POWI, where the core AC-DC market faces slower structural growth. Third, Navitas's not-meaningful P/E reflects a GaN-first architecture that is longer-dated to scale — VICR's IDM model, for all its fixed-cost risk, provides revenue clarity that pre-profitability GaN companies cannot match.

## Cash-Flow Trajectory Implied by the Current Price

A simplified reverse DCF framing — working backward from the indicative enterprise value of approximately $2.7 billion — suggests the market is crediting roughly $220–280 million in stabilised free cash flow within four to six years, assuming a 10% discount rate and a modest terminal growth rate of 3–4%. On a revenue base of $460–530 million with gross margins expanding toward 48–52% as AI product mix improves and Andover utilisation increases, and with operating expense leverage generating EBIT margins in the 22–28% range, the implied FCF target is achievable — but it requires the AI revenue conversion to proceed substantially as designed. A failure to convert the Blackwell and forward-generation Nvidia programme design-ins to volume shipments within twelve to eighteen months of this snapshot would put the implied cash-flow trajectory materially out of reach.

## Bull, Base, and Bear Scenarios

**Bull case — $90–110 per share.** The bull scenario credits three simultaneous delivery events: (1) Nvidia Rubin/Vera-Rubin rack programmes adopt Vicor's 800V HVDC power architecture at meaningful attach rates through 2026–2027, lifting revenue toward $580–650 million by FY2027; (2) Andover capacity expansion, executed on schedule, supports gross margin expansion toward 52–55% as AI module mix dominates; (3) automotive 48V design-ins begin contributing meaningful revenue. On these assumptions, forward EV/EBITDA of 28–32x and EV/Revenue of 8–9x are supportable — consistent with peak-cycle MPWR multiples applied to a structurally differentiated franchise. The resulting share price range of $90–110 implies roughly 40–70% upside from mid-range current estimates.

**Base case — $60–75 per share.** The base scenario assumes AI design-in conversion proceeds but unevenly: 48V VRM volumes at Nvidia and hyperscaler OEM customers grow through 2026, FY2026 revenue reaches $460–510 million, and operating margins expand to 20–24%. Patent litigation defence costs remain a meaningful expense headwind. Multiples drift modestly upward from current levels as revenue delivery reduces execution risk, but VICR does not re-rate to MPWR-comparable multiples absent fabless-model gross-margin comparability. The base case implies roughly 5–20% upside from current estimates — a reasonable reward for a structurally sound thesis with meaningful execution dependencies.

**Bear case — $38–50 per share.** The bear scenario centres on AI design-in slippage. If hyperscaler customers delay or reduce Vicor power-module attach on next-generation GPU programmes — substituting internally developed power solutions or competing silicon from Infineon or Monolithic Power — FY2026 revenue disappoints at $360–390 million, roughly flat with FY2025. Operating leverage fails to materialise, and patent litigation expense weighs further on earnings. Multiple compression toward 18–22x forward P/E and EV/EBITDA of 14–17x reflects a market repricing the AI thesis as aspirational rather than operational. The bear case implies 25–40% downside.

## The Gap Between Consensus and the Dossier's Read

The principal tension in Vicor's valuation is the lag between design-win disclosure and revenue recognition. The market, through the frozen-snapshot window, appears to be assigning meaningful probability to the bull path — reflected in a forward multiple above the company's own five-year median — while simultaneously demanding a discount to pure-play power-management IC peers who have already delivered AI revenue in volume.

The dossier's read is that this positioning is broadly correct but underweights one specific risk: the 800V HVDC architecture adoption timeline. The 48V intermediate-bus thesis has been partially validated; the 800V HVDC thesis remains one to two generations ahead of volume deployment. If the market begins pricing Vicor as primarily an 800V HVDC story before that architecture transitions from reference design to procurement order, multiple volatility will remain elevated regardless of near-term 48V delivery. The base case accordingly rests on 48V volume execution, not 800V optionality — treating the latter as a free call option embedded in a franchise that has earned the right to be present at the next architecture inflection.

chapters.title: Quarterly cadence through AI data center inflection and patent litigation milestones
chapters.body:
## The Revenue Cycle and the AI Inflection, 2022–2025

Vicor entered 2022 riding one of its strongest cyclical tailwinds in a decade. Demand across industrial automation, defence electronics, and an early wave of high-performance compute programmes pushed revenues to $88.3m in the first quarter — a year-on-year acceleration that management attributed to broad backlog conversion rather than any single end-market. Revenue climbed through the second and third quarters, reaching $102.2m and $103.1m respectively, before a year-end flush carried full-year 2022 revenues to approximately $399m, among the highest totals in the company's four-decade history. The period also coincided with the inauguration of Vicor's expanded Andover manufacturing campus: a 95,000-square-foot addition to its ChiP fabrication facility, funded from the balance sheet without recourse to external capital, and engineered to hold approximately $1bn of annualised production capacity at full utilisation. The company simultaneously achieved vertical integration of key outsourced process steps, compressing ChiP cycle times to as little as ten days and driving mass-production test yields to 96 percent — metrics Vinciarelli cited as structural cost advantages over fabless competitors.

The peak did not hold. Through 2023 a broad inventory correction rippled across Vicor's industrial and communications customer base. Revenues for the full year reached $405.1m, a modest gain on the prior year, but the quarterly trajectory told a more cautious story: first-quarter 2023 revenues of $97.8m declined sequentially from the Q4 2022 high before partially recovering to $107.8m by the third quarter, as hyperscaler and high-performance-compute customers began placing orders against Vicor's [Factorized Power Architecture](https://www.vicorpower.com) products for a new generation of AI accelerator rack designs. By the third quarter Vinciarelli was describing the emerging AI data-centre opportunity with characteristic precision, pointing to the thermodynamic and electrical physics constraints that he argued made Vicor's architecture uniquely suited to powering next-generation GPU and tensor-processor clusters. "This is a once in a lifetime development in terms of its significance for AI and high end computing," he told analysts.

## The ITC Filing: Turning the Patents into Leverage

Parallel to the product transition, Vicor initiated what would become its most consequential patent-enforcement campaign. On 13 July 2023, the company filed a complaint at the US International Trade Commission alleging that Delta Electronics and a cohort of contract manufacturers were importing non-isolated bus converter (NBC) modules and computing systems containing those modules in violation of US Patent Nos. 9,166,481, 9,516,761, and 10,199,950 — patents covering, respectively, the control architecture, thermal symmetry, and fixed-ratio soft-switching topology that Vicor had been developing since the mid-2000s. The ITC formally instituted [Investigation No. 337-TA-1370](https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2025/02/14/3026816/0/en/ITC-bars-importation-of-power-modules-and-unlicensed-computing-systems-that-infringe-Vicor-patents.html) on 17 August 2023, naming power converter modules destined for AI accelerators, tensor processing units, GPUs, and CPUs as the articles at issue.

Delta moved quickly to challenge the patents' validity: in November 2023 it filed an *inter partes* review petition against the '950 patent at the Patent Trial and Appeal Board. The PTAB's response, issued on 17 May 2024, was unambiguous. Having determined that Delta had not established a reasonable likelihood of prevailing in its invalidity challenge, the board denied institution — a significant early endorsement of Vicor's patent position. Separately, in May 2024 the PTAB [rejected invalidity challenges](https://www.vicorpower.com/press-room/2024/vicor-patents-asserted-against-infringing-nbms-withstand-validity-challenges) against the NBC patents more broadly, allowing the case to proceed toward a merits determination.

## FY2024: The Trough, and the Cost of Fighting

The litigation year was also a year of financial turbulence. Full-year 2024 revenues fell 11.4 percent to $359.1m, as the inventory correction deepened and a subset of hyperscaler customers deferred near-term procurement decisions pending resolution of supply-chain uncertainty around the patent dispute. The first quarter of 2024 was the weakest, at $83.9m, before a sequential recovery carried the fourth quarter to $96.2m. Gross margin improved slightly to 51.2 percent — helped by a rising mix of royalty revenue, which reached $46.6m for the year, approximately 13 percent of total revenues — but operating income collapsed from $51.4m in 2023 to an operating loss of $(1.3)m, reflecting a $19.5m litigation-contingency expense booked in the period. Full-year diluted EPS landed at $0.14, against $1.17 the prior year.

Against that earnings compression, Vicor's balance sheet provided stability that a leveraged competitor could not have sustained: cash and equivalents stood at approximately $267.6m at the end of the third quarter, funded entirely by retained earnings and prior-period operating cash flows, with no meaningful long-term debt. Vinciarelli had long maintained that vertical manufacture and a debt-free capital structure were not conservatism but strategic design — the option value of self-funded capacity expansion and protracted litigation unavailable to asset-light peers.

On the technology front, the year ended with a significant disclosure. In the third-quarter earnings call Vicor described being "close to initial deliveries of second-generation, high-density VPD systems for leading AI applications" — Gen 5 Vertical Power Delivery modules engineered to deliver current density of five amperes per square millimetre, roughly three times the capability of prior generations, at conversion efficiencies above 98 percent. Phil Davies, vice-president of global sales and marketing, confirmed that the architecture's performance targets had been met or exceeded: "Our Gen 5 vertical power delivery solution is coming to fruition with a current density exceeding its original target specification."

## The ITC Final Determination

On 27 September 2024, Administrative Law Judge Cameron Elliot of the ITC issued an Initial Determination finding a Section 337 violation: that computing systems containing infringing power converter modules, imported by Delta Electronics and contract manufacturers including Quanta Computer and Foxconn affiliates, infringed the asserted claims of Patent Nos. 9,516,761 and 9,166,481. The commission's Final Determination followed on [13 February 2025](https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2025/02/14/3026816/0/en/ITC-bars-importation-of-power-modules-and-unlicensed-computing-systems-that-infringe-Vicor-patents.html), confirming both patents valid and infringed and issuing a Limited Exclusion Order against all respondents — Delta Electronics (Americas) Ltd., Quanta Computer USA Inc. and Quanta Computer Inc., FII USA Inc., and Ingrasys Technology USA Inc. — together with Cease and Desist orders blocking domestic sales by the named parties.

The financial mechanics of the remedy were severe for any respondent seeking to continue shipments during the mandatory sixty-day presidential review period: the ITC set the bond at 100 percent of the value of the computing system, not merely the power module. In a practical sense, that imposed prohibitive carrying costs on any unlicensed system containing an infringing NBC. Vinciarelli stated that "certain OEM and non-OEM customers of infringing contract manufacturers have taken licenses" in response to the importation risk — a formulation that pointed to off-balance-sheet licensing discussions already underway with hyperscalers and OEMs that depended on the supply chains the exclusion orders had disrupted.

One wrinkle in the Final Determination gave Vicor cause for appeal: the commission reversed a prior finding and concluded that two Foxconn affiliates — FII USA, Inc. and Ingrasys Technology, Inc. — held a valid licence to the '761 patent. Vicor announced its intention to challenge that ruling at the Federal Circuit and to pursue monetary damages in parallel proceedings in the Eastern District of Texas.

## FY2025: Settlement, Recovery, and a Record Year

The legal leverage translated into cash with notable speed. In May 2025, Vicor executed settlement agreements resolving various lawsuits, arbitrations, and appeals related to the same IP cluster. The resulting $45m cash receipt was recognised in the second quarter as a patent litigation settlement, inflating Q2 2025 total revenues to $141.0m — a 64.3 percent year-on-year increase — and lifting Q2 gross margin to 65.3 percent, up 1,810 basis points sequentially. CFO Jim Schmidt noted that absent the settlement, underlying product revenue had increased by approximately $2m sequentially, reflecting steady but not yet explosive volume ramp. Schmidt also confirmed that "approximately $200 million in returns are locked in so far through March 2026" from the combined patent programme, a figure that framed the settlement as a partial rather than final monetisation.

The first quarter of 2025 had already signalled improving momentum: revenues of $94.0m rose 12 percent from Q1 2024's $83.9m, while the backlog expanded 14.2 percent year-on-year to $171.7m — a forward indicator that Vinciarelli used to anchor his forecast of record product revenues for the full year. Third-quarter revenues of $110.4m included what management described as a catch-up in royalty billings following the settlement, before moderating to $107.3m in the fourth quarter as the normalised royalty run-rate settled. Full-year 2025 product revenues reached $350.3m, a 4.1 percent gain over 2024, while royalty revenues of $57.4m (excluding the $45m settlement) rose 23.2 percent. Total revenues, including the settlement, were approximately $452.7m. Net income recovered sharply to $118.6m, or $2.61 per diluted share — against $6.1m and $0.14 in the prior year — and operating cash flow of $139.5m was 174.5 percent higher than FY2024. The cash position at year-end stood at $402.8m.

## The Forward Geometry: Gen 5, 800V, and a Second Fab

The Q4 2025 earnings call, held in February 2026, mapped the technology and capital trajectory with unusual specificity. Davies disclosed that a new 800-volt power module — enabling direct conversion from the emerging 800V HVDC distribution rails increasingly specified by hyperscaler rack architects — would begin sampling in Q4 2025, adding a second conversion tier to Vicor's data-centre architecture alongside its established 48V point-of-load product family. Vinciarelli described the strategic logic: "The reason why generations of GPUs have not been able to meet expectations has nothing to do with 400 volts or 800 volts. They have to do with the point of load." The remark encapsulated the company's positioning — that the constraint binding AI compute performance was power density and efficiency at the chip boundary, not the upstream bus voltage, and that Vicor's ChiP-packaged FPA products addressed that constraint more directly than any competing topology.

Sources: [SEC EDGAR VICR 10-K FY2024](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0000751978/000095017025030619/vicr-20241231.htm); [Vicor Q4 2025 earnings release](https://www.stocktitan.net/news/VICR/vicor-corporation-reports-results-for-the-fourth-quarter-and-year-rl9lbnjhba32.html)

On capacity, Vinciarelli projected that the first ChiP fab would approach 80 percent utilisation — which he described as the operationally prudent ceiling — "within a year," implying an annualised revenue run-rate from product and licensing of "slightly above a billion dollars." He simultaneously disclosed planning for a second fabrication facility, with a capital range of $250m to $900m depending on build-out sequencing, and stated that the company's $402.8m cash position and anticipated free-cash-flow generation gave it "the wherewithal to handle on its own." The ITC had in parallel instituted a second investigation, again involving non-isolated bus converters, extending the legal perimeter around the architecture that underpins that capacity thesis.

> "We do expect '25 to be a revenue record year," Vinciarelli told analysts in July 2025, before the full-year result confirmed the forecast. Looking further forward, he characterised the patent-settlement receipts in the context of the broader opportunity: "The $45,000,000 event last year is another drop in the bucket."

The cadence of the four-year period — a cyclical peak, a corrective trough compounded by litigation expense, a patent enforcement victory, and a licensing-accelerated recovery — traced a pattern Vinciarelli had navigated before, across earlier generations of Vicor IP enforcement. What distinguished the 2022–2025 cycle was the convergence of the litigation arc with the AI-data-centre demand inflection: an architecture conceived in the 1990s, refined for a decade in Andover, and now sitting at the intersection of the two most powerful currents in the global semiconductor and systems supply chain.

chapters.title: Patrizio Vinciarelli, CFO, executive team, and the board
chapters.body:
## The Physicist at the Helm

Before Patrizio Vinciarelli wrote his first power-conversion patent, he was tracing the behaviour of quarks.

Vinciarelli earned his doctorate in physics from Sapienza University of Rome, then spent three years from 1973 to 1976 as a Fellow at CERN in Geneva, where his research centred on soliton models of hadrons — the quark-confinement problem at the high-energy frontier. He moved to Princeton in 1977 as a Fellow at the Institute for Advanced Study, the storied think-tank where Einstein had spent his American years, and simultaneously served as an instructor at Princeton University through 1980. He had, by that point, published in more than 40 academic papers and accumulated the intellectual apparatus of a theoretical physicist comfortable working at the boundary of the known.

The pivot from particle physics to power electronics was not random. The high-energy experiments Vinciarelli worked with at CERN required precision power supplies operating at frequencies and power densities that the technology of the 1970s simply could not reliably deliver. The inefficiency was not a peripheral concern but a bottleneck at the scientific frontier — and Vinciarelli, trained to find the elegant solution at the intersection of theory and experiment, began working on a better approach.

On April 2, 1981, he incorporated Vicor Corporation in Massachusetts to commercialise a novel Zero Current Switching topology — a technique that enabled power conversion at significantly higher frequencies than conventional designs, slashing switching losses and permitting far smaller, denser converters. The topology was genuinely new: the kind of insight that only a physicist habituated to building from first principles would formulate in a market populated largely by engineers optimising incremental improvements to existing circuits.

## Forty-Four Years of Founder Control

The 1990 NASDAQ IPO put Vicor on the public markets, but it did not meaningfully dilute Vinciarelli's grip on the company he had spent a decade building. As of the March 31, 2026 record date disclosed in [Vicor's most recent DEF 14A proxy statement](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0000751978/000095017025060646/vicr-20250430.htm), Vinciarelli held 9,156,109 shares of common stock and 11,023,648 shares of Class B common stock, which carry ten votes per share against the one-vote-per-share ordinary common — giving him 79.1 percent of total voting power over a company with 33.8 million common shares and 11.7 million Class B shares outstanding. Class B shares are convertible into common stock at the holder's election but carry no automatic conversion trigger; the structure will persist as long as Vinciarelli chooses to preserve it.

The arithmetic makes Vicor's governance posture explicit. Under Nasdaq's controlled-company rules, a stockholder controlling more than 50 percent of voting power removes the company from certain board independence mandates. Vicor disclosed in its 2025 proxy that it relies on those exemptions — though it has maintained fully independent audit and compensation committees across market cycles, a governance floor it has consistently preserved.

No institutional campaign, no activist proxy contest, no board challenge can reorient Vicor without Vinciarelli's consent. He has been chairman, president, and chief executive officer since the April 1981 founding — a tenure of 44-plus years that places him among the longest-serving founder-CEOs in the U.S.-listed electronics universe. Age 79 as of the April 2026 proxy, he still runs quarterly earnings calls, fields analyst questions in detail, and holds inventor-of-record status on a patent portfolio that by the time of the 2025 proxy had grown to more than 150 patents for power-conversion technology. His total compensation for 2025, as disclosed in the proxy, was $702,202 — a figure that places him below the median for even mid-cap technology CEOs, and reflects a founder's structural preference for equity appreciation over cash extraction.

> "Our lead in power density and current density has been expanding for four decades."

The statement, made in a published interview, is characteristic of the way Vinciarelli frames Vicor's competitive position — as the compound consequence of sustained research investment rather than a product-cycle advantage that any well-funded rival could replicate.

## Patent Inventor as Chief Executive

Vinciarelli's name appears as inventor of record on the foundational patents Vicor has defended in multi-year litigation against competitors — covering Zero Current Switching, Factorized Power Architecture structures, ChiP packaging geometries, and the Network Bus Module (NBM) topologies central to the 48V AI data-centre architecture transition. The patent franchise is not a legacy asset. When Vinciarelli addressed the Q4 2025 earnings call, CFO James F. Schmidt disclosed $57.4 million in royalty revenues for the year — excluding a separate litigation settlement — and Vinciarelli described a licensing pipeline he expected to double within a couple of years. His position on infringement is unequivocal:

> "There is no known NBM alternative that doesn't infringe on our patents."

When pressed on the identity of an undisclosed AI infrastructure customer that had agreed to license Vicor's NBM patents on Vicor's Q4 2024 earnings call, he offered only this:

> "I can't tell you anything beyond the fact that it's a hyperscaler, and it's a significant license."

The characteristic opacity — providing investors exactly what the law requires and no more — is consistent with how he has communicated for four decades.

## The CFO: James F. Schmidt

James F. Schmidt joined Vicor as corporate vice president, chief financial officer, treasurer, and corporate secretary in June 2021, arriving from Analog Devices, where he had spent the prior years following an arc through wafer fabrication operations that began in 1984. His Analog Devices tenure included the role of vice president for global broad market and sales operations from 2017 to 2020, and senior director of global business controller from 2013 to 2017 — a sequence that gave him experience in both financial reporting and the operational realities of a vertically-integrated analog semiconductor company. He holds a B.S. in Chemical Engineering from the University of Cincinnati and an M.B.A. from the University of North Carolina at Greensboro. His total 2025 compensation was $670,166, a figure approximately in line with Vinciarelli's own cash-based package — an unusual relationship at most public companies, where CEO-to-CFO pay gaps tend to be considerably wider.

Schmidt's background in engineering before finance is a pattern Vicor's hiring has favoured: at a company whose competitive advantages are rooted in fabrication technology, functional managers who can read a process flow alongside a balance sheet carry operational credibility in internal capital-allocation decisions that finance-track executives typically do not.

## A Board Designed Around the Technology

The board that stood for election at the 2026 annual meeting comprised eleven directors. Four were fully independent under Nasdaq standards; six were company officers or affiliates not classified as independent. The composition is a direct artifact of the controlled-company structure: with Vinciarelli holding 79 percent of votes, the board functions less as a check on management than as a domain-expert advisory council assembled by a founder who has consistently hired for technical depth over governance optics.

The independent directors repay close examination. Estia J. Eichten has served on the board since 1981 — the company's founding year — and holds MIT physics degrees; he is a Senior Scientist Emeritus at Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory, a parallel academic trajectory to Vinciarelli's own, and separately holds 5.9 percent of the Class B stock, aligning his interests more economically than fiduciarily. Jason L. Carlson chairs the audit committee, carries the audit committee financial expert designation, and is a former chief executive of congatec AG, a European embedded computing company; he has served since 2008. Zmira Lavie joined in 2022, bringing thirty-plus years of semiconductor manufacturing experience including a stint as SVP and general manager at Tower Semiconductor. John Shen, also a 2022 addition, is an IEEE Fellow with 18 U.S. patents, holds degrees from Tsinghua University and Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute, and directs a power electronics research programme at Simon Fraser University — one of the few board members outside Vicor's own organisation who can evaluate an FPA topology drawing on its technical merits.

The non-independent directors reflect Vicor's organisational ethos of promoting from within. Claudio Tuozzolo, on the board since 2007, became president of Vicor Power Components in 2018 following fifteen years running the Picor subsidiary and holds 9 U.S. patents; he brings product-line P&L accountability to the table. Michael S. McNamara has run operations since 2015, with a quality and manufacturing career at the company stretching back to 1995, and joined the board in 2019. Andrew T. D'Amico has served as general counsel for IP matters since 2006, holds a B.S. in electrical engineering alongside his law degree, and became a director in 2020 — a combination that makes him structurally indispensable given the scale of Vicor's ongoing patent-enforcement programme. Philip D. Davies, who joined the board in 2019, oversees global sales and marketing and previously held vice-president roles at Analog Devices and NoblePeak Vision. Samuel J. Anderson, on the board since 2001, is the chief executive of IceMOS Technology and a former Motorola and ON Semiconductor executive with his own semiconductor patent portfolio.

The result is a board where semiconductor process engineers, patent attorneys, IEEE Fellows, and physicists of long standing sit alongside the company's senior operational managers. There is no general-purpose retail executive, no fintech operator, no brand-management consultant among the eleven. Vicor's board is, almost entirely, a power electronics board.

## Founder as Institution

The governance architecture Vinciarelli has maintained across 44 years is the logical extension of the company he built. Vicor is not organised to maximise near-term earnings guidance or to smooth quarterly sell-side expectations; it is organised to develop and defend a compounding technology franchise across long R&D cycles. The dual-class share structure, the controlled-company designation, the inside-heavy board, and the below-market executive pay all point toward the same conclusion: this is a company run by its founder as a scientific project with commercial ambitions, and where the governance apparatus has been built to protect that project rather than to constrain it.

That posture carries risk. At 79, Vinciarelli has disclosed no formal succession plan in any SEC filing as of the frozen snapshot date of May 23, 2026. The proxy lists no president-in-waiting, no COO with an articulated transition mandate. The interlocking dependencies — founder as chairman, president, CEO, principal patent inventor, and controlling stockholder — mean that governance continuity is structurally inseparable from Vinciarelli himself. For investors who regard the Factorized Power Architecture and ChiP IP franchise as a multi-decade asset, that concentration is simultaneously the source of the company's strategic coherence and its most conspicuous single-point-of-failure risk.

---

*Sources: [Vicor DEF 14A (FY2025), SEC EDGAR](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0000751978/000095017025060646/vicr-20250430.htm); [Vicor 10-K FY2024, SEC EDGAR](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/751978/000095017025030619/vicr-20241231.htm); [Patrizio Vinciarelli, Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrizio_Vinciarelli); Q4 2024 and Q3–Q4 2025 earnings call transcripts.*

chapters.title: AI hyperscalers, server OEMs, defense, industrial, automotive 48V
chapters.body:
## The Hyperscale Inflection: Nvidia, 48V, and the AI Power Stack

The demand signal that restructured Vicor's commercial trajectory arrived not as a single contract but as an architectural mandate.
